answers.output: 似然和后验回答两个不同的问题，方向别搞反。似然问：假设某假设为真，看到眼前这批数据的可能性多大，记作P(数据|假设)；后验问：看到数据后，这假设成立的概率多大，P(假设|数据)。例子：连抛3次全是正面。若硬币公平，P(3正|公平)=(1/2)³=1/8；若两面都是正面，P(3正|全正)=1。这两个都是似然，用来比较假设，不是假设为真的概率。别因此断定硬币必是全正面：后验还要乘上先验。全正面硬币本就极罕见，设P(全正)=1/1000，后验≈(1×0.001)/(1×0.001+1/8×0.999)≈0.008，仍很小。贝叶斯公式就是「似然×先验」归一化后得到后验。数据固定不动，变动的是假设——这正是似然的用法。

answers.output: Variance measures how far numbers spread around their average. Recipe: take each value's distance from the mean, square it, average the squares. Example: scores {2, 4, 6}. Mean = 4; distances −2, 0, +2; squares 4, 0, 4; variance = 8/3 ≈ 2.67. Why square the distances? Raw distances always sum to zero (−2+0+2=0) — positives and negatives cancel, hiding the spread. Squaring also punishes big deviations hard: change 6 to 10 and variance jumps from 2.67 to about 11.6, while the mean only moves from 4 to 5.3. The cost: units get squared (points²), so we usually take the square root — the standard deviation — to return to original units. Two classes with the same mean but very different variances are very different in consistency.

answers.output: Cache invalidation is deciding when a stored copy of data is too stale to serve. A web app keeps the product price in memory so pages render without hitting the database. The risk: the price changes in the database, but the cache still says $50, so customers see outdated data. Strategies trade freshness against speed. TTL: expire entries after, say, 60 seconds — simple, but up to a minute of staleness. Write-through: update or delete the cache entry whenever the database is written — fresher, but every write pays extra cost, and a missed write leaves stale data anyway. The hard part is you can't always know when underlying data changed, hence the joke that cache invalidation is one of the two hard problems in CS. Condition change: rarely-changing data (product titles) tolerates long TTLs; flash-sale prices need immediate invalidation.

answers.output: Compound growth means growth earns growth: each period's gain is added to the base, so the next gain is bigger. $1,000 at 10%: year 1 → $1,100; year 2 → $1,210; year 3 → $1,331. After n years: 1000 × 1.1ⁿ — each year multiplies rather than adds. Why the starting amount matters: multiplication is proportional, so the same rate on $2,000 doubles every result ($2,662 vs $1,331 after 3 years) with zero extra effort. Time compounds the same way: the last decade of a 40-year investment dwarfs the first, because late gains act on a large base. Condition change: at 5% instead of 10%, $1,000 reaches only about $1,158 in 3 years — rate, base, and time each enter multiplicatively, so none can be judged alone.

Two datasets can share the same average and differ completely in spread. {4, 5, 6} and {0, 5, 10} both average 5, but the second varies far more. Population variance measures that spread: take each value's deviation from the mean, square it, and average: variance = mean of (x − μ)².

For {4,5,6}: deviations −1, 0, 1; variance = (1+0+1)/3 ≈ 0.67. For {0,5,10}: (25+0+25)/3 ≈ 16.7. Squaring matters: raw deviations always sum to zero, so they would cancel out; squaring keeps them positive and punishes large deviations harder.

Consequences: one extreme value can dominate the variance for the same reason, and the units are squared—so √variance (the standard deviation) puts the number back in original units. "Population" means you divide by N, all members. Change any single data point and the mean shifts too, so every deviation moves.

Opportunity cost is the value of the best option you give up—not all options combined. Free afternoon: nap, gym, or study. You pick the gym; your opportunity cost is the single best alternative forgone (say, studying), not nap plus study. Money already spent on a gym membership is a sunk cost and should not enter the comparison.

The framing matters because "free" time is rarely free: an hour spent here is an hour not spent there. Condition change: if an exam is tomorrow, studying's value rises, so the cost of choosing the gym rises and may flip your decision. Watch the boundary: comparing three options does not triple the cost—the lower-valued ones never enter the tally.

Transfer: staying in a comfortable job looks costless, but the growth and pay you would forgo elsewhere are real costs. Whenever you choose, ask what the next-best use of that hour is.

answers.output:
A cache is a fast copy of slow data. Your user profile lives in a database; after the first read, the app keeps it in Redis so later visits skip the slow query. The copy speeds things up—and creates a new problem: when the profile changes in the database, the cache still holds the old value, and users see stale data.

Cache invalidation is how you fix that: remove or refresh cached entries when the underlying data changes. Main options: (1) TTL—expire entries after N seconds; simple, but data is stale until expiry. (2) Delete-on-write—when the database row updates, delete the cache key; the next read repopulates with fresh data. (3) Write-through—update cache and database together.

Each has costs: delete-on-write adds code and a failure mode (the cache delete can fail after the database update commits). TTL alone guarantees only eventual freshness. The same problem recurs at every layer—CDNs and browser caches all hold copies that must be told when the source changed.

Compound growth: your gains start earning gains. $1,000 at 10% per year grows to $1,100, and next year the 10% applies to $1,100, not $1,000. After n years: 1000 × 1.1ⁿ—about $2,594 after 10 years, not the $2,000 linear growth would give. The gap is interest earned on interest, and it widens every year.

Why the starting amount matters: the formula is multiplicative, so the same rate and time scale whatever you begin with. Start with $4,000 and you end with 4× as much. answers.output: A cache keeps a copy of data close by so requests skip the slow original — but a copy goes stale when the original changes. Cache invalidation is removing or refreshing stale copies. Your product page reads 'price of item #7' from the database on every visit; you cache the answer for an hour and 10,000 visits skip the database. The merchant then cuts the price — until something happens, visitors see the old number. Options: (1) TTL — accept staleness and let the entry expire; simple, wrong in the gap. (2) Invalidate on write — when the price updates, delete the cached key 'price:7'; the next visitor re-fetches fresh data. Accurate, but every write path must do it, including admin tools and batch jobs, or the stale copy survives. This is why invalidation is famously hard: the same data may sit in many places — browser, CDN, app server — and one write must reach them all. The rule of thumb: tolerated staleness picks the mechanism — prices users compare need write-time invalidation; view counts can live with a TTL.

Formula: final = start × (1+r)^t. $1,000 at 7% a year reaches about $1,967 in 10 years and $7,612 in 30 — the jumps accelerate because the same percentage applies to an ever-larger base. The ratio stays 10×, but the absolute gap widens from $9,000 to $68,511 — the bigger base earns more dollars per year at the same percentage. That's why growing the base early beats chasing the rate: time sits in the exponent. Caveats: the formula assumes a constant rate and untouched principal. answers.output: Variance measures how spread out numbers are around their average: the mean of squared deviations. Take 2, 4, 6 with mean 4. Each number deviates by −2, 0, +2. If you averaged the deviations themselves, they'd cancel to zero and tell you nothing — so we square each one first: 4, 0, 4, then average: 8/3 ≈ 2.67. That's the population variance, dividing by N because these are all the numbers. Squaring solves cancellation but does two more things: it treats deviations above and below the mean identically, and it punishes large deviations disproportionately — one value far from the mean raises variance much more than several slightly-off values do. Since squaring changes units, the square root (standard deviation, here ≈ 1.63) is what you compare against the original data's scale.

answers.output: Cache invalidation is deciding when a stored copy of data no longer matches the source and must be deleted or refreshed. A web app caches a product's price so each page view doesn't hit the database. When the store updates that price, every cached copy is now wrong — the app must invalidate it (delete it so the next request reloads fresh data) or it will show customers outdated prices. Computing it: take each value's distance from the mean — for {1,3,5}: -2, 0, +2. Plain distances cancel out (they always sum to zero, which is what an average guarantees), so we square them: 4, 0, 4. Squaring fixes the cancellation and also emphasizes large deviations. Then average the squares: (4+0+4)/3 ≈ 2.67. That's the population variance — dividing by 3 because we have all three values.

Change one value to {1,3,11} and the mean moves to 5 while variance jumps to about 18.7: a single outlier dominates.

Variance is in squared units, so taking its square root gives the standard deviation, back in the original units — the typical distance from the mean.

Opportunity cost is the value of the best option you give up when you pick one. Your free afternoon has three realistic uses: rest, study for Monday's exam, or hike. If you hike, the cost is not 'everything else' — it's the single best foregone option, say studying, which you expect to raise your grade. That benefit is what hiking really costs you, even though no money changes hands; time is the resource, and spending it one way means it can't be spent another.

So the decision question becomes: is the hike worth more to me than the next best use of those hours? Two cautions: only count real alternatives (if you'd never have studied anyway, that's not the cost), and ignore anything already spent earlier — sunk costs don't belong in this afternoon's comparison.

核心问题：检测出阳性后，真患病的概率是多少？答案是约17%，远低于检测准确率。贝叶斯公式解释了为什么。

设10000人体检，患病率1%：
- 患者100人，检测准确率99%，阳性约99人；
- 健康人9900人，误报率5%，阳性约495人。

阳性总人数 99+495=594。拿到阳性的人里，真正患病的比例是 99/594 ≈ 16.7%。

写成公式：P(患病|阳性) = P(患病)×P(阳性|患病) ÷ P(阳性)。分子是'真患者中被检出阳性的部分'，分母是'所有阳性者'，这就是贝叶斯公式。

关键在患病率这个起点：同样99%的准确率，患病率降到千分之一时，阳性后真患病的概率只有约2%。阳性的意义是把怀疑从1%提到17%，要确认还得复检——复检时你的起点已经是17%了。

A cache keeps a copy of expensive data in fast storage: the product page's price is read from the database once, stored in Redis, and the next thousand visitors use the copy instead of hitting the database.

The problem: when the real price changes, the copy still shows the old one. Cache invalidation means deciding when a copy is no longer trustworthy and must be dropped or refreshed.

Two common strategies. TTL: each entry gets a lifetime, say 60 seconds — simple, but for up to a minute users see stale prices. Delete-on-write: when the price updates, delete the cache key, so the next read refetches fresh data.

The hard part is knowing everything that depends on what you changed. The price shows up on the product page, the category listing, the search index, another service's cache — miss one and some users see stale data indefinitely. That's why cache invalidation is famous as a genuinely hard problem.

Compound growth means each period's gain is a percentage of the current total, so past gains start earning their own gains.

Put 1,000 yuan at 10% per year. Year 1: 1,100. Year 2: interest is 10% of 1,100 — 110, not 100 — giving 1,210. Year 3: 1,331. Simple interest would pay 300 in total; compounding pays 331, and the gap widens every year because the base keeps growing. The formula is principal × (1 + rate)^years.

Why the starting amount matters: everything gets multiplied by the same factor, so proportions are identical but absolute gains scale with the base. After five years, 1,000 becomes 1,611 while 10,000 becomes 16,105 — the extra 9,000 you started with was itself invested and compounded.

Starting time works the same way: each extra year adds one more multiplication. At 7% per year, ten extra years roughly doubles the final amount.

answers.output: A cache keeps a nearby copy of data so requests avoid a slow trip to the database. The copy goes stale when the real data changes, so the system must invalidate it — drop the copy or refresh it. Say a product's price rises from $9 to $10 in the database but the cache still serves $9; users see wrong prices at checkout. Common strategies: TTL (expire the copy after N seconds — simple, but with a window of staleness); delete-on-write (drop the key when data changes, next read repopulates it); write-through (update cache and database together). The hard part in distributed systems is knowing exactly which copies, on which servers, at which moment — and dodging races where a stale write lands after the invalidation. That coordination burden is why cache invalidation is called one of the hard problems in computer science.

A free afternoon doesn't make choices free — spending it hiking means not spending it studying, napping, or earning money. answers.output: A cache keeps a nearby copy of data so you don't recompute or re-fetch it every time — like keeping the milk you use daily on the counter instead of running to the store. The problem: when the original changes, the copy is stale. If the store updates a price in its database but the cached page still shows the old one, customers see wrong numbers. Cache invalidation is the set of rules deciding when a cached copy must be dropped or refreshed. Two common approaches: expiry time (each copy is trusted for, say, 60 seconds — simple, but there's always a window of showing stale data), and event-based invalidation (the moment the database is written, delete the matching cache entry — accurate, but if one event is lost, the cache stays wrong indefinitely). It's famously hard because with many servers and caches, a write must correctly reach every copy, while readers may hit any of them at any moment.

Variance measures that spread — it is the average of squared distances from the mean. Steps: subtract the mean from each value, square the result, then average those squares. Squaring serves two purposes: deviations above and below the mean would cancel to exactly zero if merely summed, and squaring makes large deviations count much more than small ones. Its units are the square of the original units, so the square root (standard deviation) is reported when you want spread in the data's own units. Population variance divides by N because it assumes you have every member of the group.

answers.output: Opportunity cost is the value of the best option you give up when you choose one thing. A free afternoon: you could nap, study for Friday's exam, or play basketball. You pick basketball. The cost isn't all the other options combined — just the single best one you sacrificed, say the study session; and if rest mattered most to you, then studying was the cost. This is why "free" rarely is: even a free concert costs the afternoon you could have spent otherwise. Money needn't change hands for a cost to exist — time spent one way cannot be spent another. Watch the boundary: sunk costs don't belong in the comparison. A ticket you already bought for an event you no longer want to attend is gone either way; compare only what each option gives you going forward.

answers.output: A cache is a fast copy of slow data kept nearby — say user profiles held in memory instead of the database. Reads get quick, but you've created a copy that can go stale: when the real data changes, the copy must be thrown out or refreshed. That's cache invalidation — deciding when a stored copy is no longer trustworthy. Example: a shop caches "price: 100" for a product, then cuts the real price to 80. Until the entry is invalidated, customers see 100; if they're charged it, the stale copy caused real harm. Common strategies: delete the entry whenever the underlying data changes, or attach a time-to-live so copies expire after, say, 60 seconds — trading freshness for fewer database hits. The hard part is the stale window itself: invalidate too eagerly and the cache buys you nothing; too lazily and users act on wrong data.

answers.output: Compound growth means the gain itself earns gains: each period grows the whole current balance, not just the original amount. At 10% a year, 100 becomes 110, and next year grows by 11, not 10 — the first year's interest now counts as principal. After n years the balance is start × (1.1)ⁿ. The multiplier is identical for everyone, so all differences come from the starting amount — that's exactly why it matters: growth is proportional, so a bigger base harvests bigger absolute gains at the same rate. Start with 1000 instead of 100 and after ten years you hold 2594 versus 259; the gap widens from 900 to 2335. The same math powers epidemics and nuclear chains, and it cuts both ways: credit-card debt at 20% doubles roughly every 3.6 years. The earlier a base exists, the more rounds of multiplication it experiences.

answers.output: Two classes both average 50 on a test: in one, scores run 48–52; in the other, 10–90. The average alone can't tell them apart — that's the gap variance fills: a number for how spread out data is around the mean. Recipe: subtract the mean from each value (the deviations), square them (otherwise positives and negatives cancel to zero), then average the squares — for a whole population, divide by N. Squaring also makes big deviations dominate: {0,50,100} gives variance 2500, {49,50,51} gives about 0.67. Since units get squared, people quote the square root — the standard deviation — back in original units. Change one condition: move a 51 to a 91 and the mean barely shifts, but variance jumps — it tracks spread, not location.

answers.output: Your web page needs the user's profile on every request. Reading it from the database each time is slow, so you keep a copy in fast memory — a cache. The catch: when the data changes (say, the password is updated), the copy doesn't know. Serving the stale copy after a password change is a correctness bug; deciding when to throw away or refresh the copy is cache invalidation — famously hard because it's a bet on the future. Two common strategies: give each entry a TTL (expire after 60 seconds — simple, but stale for up to 60s), or invalidate on write — when the database row changes, delete the cache key so the next read refetches (fresher, but more wiring and race conditions to handle). Judgment: rarely-changing, read-heavy data rewards caching; hot, constantly-rewritten data lets invalidation costs eat the gains.

answers.output: Opportunity cost is the value of the best option you give up when choosing one thing—only the single best one, not everything you could have done. A free afternoon with three options: study for Monday's exam, meet a friend, nap. You choose the friend. The cost isn't 'exam plus nap'; it's whichever you'd have picked instead—say, studying. That lost prep time is the real price of the outing, though no money changed hands. Two habits follow. Count what you skip, not just what you pay: a 'free' concert still costs the afternoon. And compare honestly, because rankings can flip—if the exam decides your grade, skipping it costs too much; if you're exhausted, the forgone nap is the true cost. answers.output: Cache invalidation is deciding when a cached copy is too old to serve. A web app keeps a user's profile in memory so page views skip the database—fast, until the user changes their avatar. The database now has the new photo, the cache still holds the old one, and visitors keep seeing it until something retires that entry. Retiring it is invalidation. Caching is easy; knowing when is hard. Common choices: expire after a fixed time (simple, but stale in the meantime), delete the entry whenever the data is written (fresh, but every write must reach the cache too), or bake a version into the key so new data lands under a new name and the old copy expires harmlessly. The rule of thumb: the more a value can change unnoticed, the more invalidation costs—for a bank balance you'd invalidate on every write, or not cache at all.

answers.output: Compound growth adds each period's gain to the base, so gains earn gains: an amount P grows to P(1+r)ⁿ. At 10% a year, 10,000 becomes 11,000, then 12,100, then 13,310—the yearly gain itself grows from 1,000 to 1,100, because last year's extra 100 now earns too. After 30 years you have about 174,500, not the 40,000 simple interest would give. The starting amount matters because growth is multiplicative: it scales whatever you begin with. 100,000 and 10,000 both grow about 17-fold in those 30 years—1.75 million versus 174,500—and the gap never narrows on its own; same rate, same time, proportions preserved. Two other levers bite hard: at 7% instead of 10%, that 10,000 reaches only about 76,000; and because gains feed on earlier gains, the final decade adds more than the first—starting ten years later leaves you with about 40% of the final amount. The model assumes a steady rate; real returns fluctuate and fees cut in.

answers.output: Opportunity cost is the value of the best thing you give up — which is why a 'free' afternoon isn't free. Say your free afternoon has three options: pick up a shift for $50, study for an exam, or nap. If you choose the nap, the opportunity cost is $50, the single best option you passed up — not $50 plus the studying plus everything else; cost means the next-best alternative only. So the real question is always 'is this worth more than my best alternative?' Change one condition and the answer changes: if no shift is offered this week, napping's cost drops to whatever studying would have earned you. The same logic reaches beyond afternoons: a free concert still costs three hours, and a founder's zero-salary year costs the wage she forgoes. The true price tag of any choice is the best thing you didn't choose.

answers.output: A cache is a fast copy of slow data, and cache invalidation is deciding when that copy has gone stale. A web app keeps its truth in a database, but reading it on every page view is slow, so it caches hot items like a bestseller's price. The catch: when the price changes in the database, the cache still holds the old one, and customers see stale numbers until something fixes it. Two common policies: a TTL expires entries after, say, 60 seconds — simple, but stale for up to a minute; write-through invalidates the key the moment the database changes — fresher, but more wiring. Change the setup and new trouble appears: ten app servers each holding their own cache means updating one leaves nine stale. The hard part is the trade-off — fresher data costs more invalidation machinery — which is why cache invalidation is called one of the two genuinely hard problems in computer science.

answers.output: Caching stores a copy of expensive data (a database query result) in a faster place (Redis, memory) so requests skip the slow source. The problem: when the underlying data changes, the copy goes stale — and stale data can be worse than slow data. Cache invalidation is deciding when and how to remove or refresh that copy. Example: a product page caches its price for 5 minutes; the merchant changes the price to $50, but shoppers keep seeing $80 — a stale read for up to 5 minutes. Two common strategies: TTL — expire after a fixed time, simple, but you accept staleness up to that bound; invalidate-on-write — delete the cache entry whenever the data is updated, fresher, but you must catch every write path, and missing one leaves silent staleness (part of why the problem is famous). There's a real trade-off: stronger consistency costs coordination and speed. Condition change: a display-only price tolerates a 5-minute TTL; a price feeding checkout must come from the source of truth — correctness beats speed. Transfer: your browser caches pages via Cache-Control headers; sites bust it by versioning URLs.

answers.output: Compound growth means growth proportional to what you already have, so gains earn gains: A = P(1+r)^t. Start $1,000 at 10%/year: year 1 adds $100 → $1,100; year 2 adds $110, not $100 → $1,210; year 3 adds $121 → $1,331. Each year's gain grows because the base grows; simple interest would give only $1,300. Why the starting amount matters: the multiplier (1+r)^t is the same for everyone and the formula is linear in P. Start with $2,000 instead of $1,000 and you have exactly double at every point — an early lead compounds too; that extra $1,000 becomes about $17,450 after 30 years at 10%. Condition change: time and rate interact — doubling time ≈ 72/rate, so 10% doubles in ~7 years, 5% in ~14; halving the rate doubles the wait, and small rate gaps compound into large gaps. Caveat: a model, not a promise — real returns fluctuate and losses shrink the base. Transfer: unpaid debt compounds against you the same way.

Starting amount matters because it is the base the exponent multiplies: $2,000 at the same rate for the same time becomes ≈ $15,200 — twice the start, twice the end. But starting earlier usually matters even more: that $1,000 invested 10 years sooner reaches ≈ $1,900 extra by the same date, because the extra decade's growth also compounds. Two cautions: the formula assumes a constant rate, while real returns fluctuate; and the exponent amplifies whatever base you give it — a higher rate or longer time changes the outcome far more than intuition suggests.

answers.output: An average gives the center; variance measures how spread out the data is around that center. Two classes both average 70: one with scores 68, 70, 72; another with 40, 70, 100. Same center, very different reliability — variance captures this difference. How: subtract the mean from each value, square the results, average them: σ² = mean of (x − μ)². Why subtract? Deviations above and below the mean cancel (their sum is always zero), so raw deviations cannot measure spread. Why square? It removes the sign and punishes large deviations: a point 30 off contributes 900, a point 10 off only 100 — nine times the weight, not three. Run it: 68, 70, 72 → deviations −2, 0, 2 → variance (4+0+4)/3 ≈ 2.7. Absolute values would also fix the sign problem, but squares are mathematically easier and stress outliers. Square root gives standard deviation, back in original units. Caveat: population variance divides by N, and one extreme value moves it a lot.

answers.output: Opportunity cost is the value of the best option you give up when you choose one thing. Your afternoon offers three options: nap, gym, finish a scholarship application worth a $500 chance. If you nap, your opportunity cost is not everything else combined — it is the single best forgone option, which here is the application. The gym was also given up, but it was only your second choice, so it does not count; the cost is measured by the top alternative. answers.output: A cache keeps a copy of data close by so the app does not re-fetch or recompute it — e.g., a web app stores a rendered profile page in Redis and serves it for 60 seconds instead of hitting the database on every visit. This only works while the copy matches the real data. Cache invalidation is removing or refreshing that copy when the underlying data changes. The core problem: writes can reach the database without the cache knowing, because the cache sits between users and the database. If an admin edits the profile but the cached copy survives, users keep seeing the old page until expiry — the change appears to have failed. Common strategies: TTL (accept brief staleness, here 60 seconds); write-through (update database and cache together on every write); or delete the cache entry on write so the next read re-fetches fresh data. The trade-off is constant: fresher data costs more coordination and more database load.

answers.output: Compound growth means growth on top of past growth: each period the amount rises by a fixed percentage of the current total, not the original. At rate r for n periods, amount = P(1+r)^n. Example: 1000 at 10% becomes 1100, then 1210, then 1331 — the yearly gain itself grows (100, 110, 121) because each period's base includes all previous gains. Why the starting amount P matters: the formula just multiplies it, so growth is proportional. Starting with 10,000 at the same rate always leaves you exactly 10x someone starting with 1,000 — the rate alone never closes that gap; only a higher rate or more time changes the ratio. Condition change: if gains are withdrawn each period, growth becomes linear (simple interest: 1000 → 1100 → 1200) and the exponential gap never opens. Transfer: follower counts, compounding debt, and network effects all follow the same proportional mechanism.

answers.output: Compound growth multiplies rather than adds: each period the amount becomes (1+r) times what it was, so value = P(1+r)^t. The 'compound' part is that growth applies to the accumulated total, including past gains — interest earns interest. Numbers: $1,000 at 10% a year for 20 years becomes 1000 × 1.1²⁰ ≈ $6,727; $100 at the same rate becomes only $673. The ratio between them never shrinks, because the same multiplier 1.1²⁰ applies to both — a 10× larger start stays 10× larger. That is why the starting amount matters: rate and time decide how fast you multiply, but the principal is the base being multiplied, and all the exponential growth inherits it. Change one condition: at 7% instead of 10%, the $1,000 grows to only about $3,870 — small rate differences compound into large gaps, the same mechanism acting on the multiplier itself.

answers.output: The average tells you where a list's center sits; variance measures how spread out the values are around it. Take 2, 4, 6: mean 4, deviations −2, 0, +2. You cannot average the deviations — they always sum to zero, which would make every dataset look perfectly concentrated. Squaring prevents that cancellation: 4, 0, 4, averaged to 8/3 ≈ 2.67. Variance is the average squared distance from the mean. Squaring is a choice, not a law — absolute values would also stop cancellation — but squaring punishes large deviations much harder: one value 10 off contributes 100, while ten values 1 off contribute 10 in total. So variance is outlier-sensitive, which is either the point or the flaw depending on your question. Side effect: units get squared (kg²), so we usually report the square root, the standard deviation. Note how it scales: doubling every value's distance from the mean makes variance four times larger.

answers.output: A cache keeps a fast local copy of slow data — the server stores a product's price so it need not query the database on every page view. The catch: copy and original are separate storages, and the copy never learns on its own when the original changed. Cache invalidation is the decision about when a cached copy stops being trustworthy and must be dropped or refreshed. Example: the page is cached for 5 minutes, the team cuts the price, and for up to 5 minutes customers see the old figure — possibly checking out at a stale amount. Two common policies: a TTL simply expires copies after N seconds — simple, but freshness is only guaranteed up to N; or the write path actively deletes the cache entry when the price changes, so the next read refetches — fresher, but writes now touch two systems. It is called a hard problem because at scale copies live in many places; updating one leaves the others serving stale data.

answers.output: Compound growth is growth on growth: each period's gain is computed on the running total, not the original amount. $1,000 at 10% a year becomes $1,100, then $1,210, then $1,331 — after t years, 1,000 × 1.1^t. Everyone's multiplier 1.1^t is the same; only the starting principal scales it. That is why the start matters: $100 at the same rate becomes $259 in ten years while $1,000 becomes $2,594 — the tenfold gap never closes by itself, because a fixed rate multiplies whatever you have. Starting earlier works through the exponent instead: $1,000 invested at 25 rather than 35 gives, at 65, about $45,300 versus $17,400 — ten extra years nearly tripled it. Time cuts both ways: over a few years compounding barely bites and small rate differences hardly matter; over forty years, 7% versus 5% more than doubles the gap in outcome. The judgment to carry: check the horizon before weighing any rate.

answers.output: Variance answers: how spread out is data around its average? The mean alone hides spread — {2,4,6} and {0,4,8} both average 4, but the second varies far more. answers.output: Opportunity cost is the value of the best option you give up when you choose one thing. Suppose your free afternoon has three uses: nap, study for Friday's exam, or tutor for $50. If you pick studying, the opportunity cost isn't all rejected options — only the best one you passed up, say the $50 tutoring. That hidden price is the real comparison: choose studying only if its value to you beats $50. Two common mistakes: counting money spent as the whole cost (time counts too, even for free activities), and adding up every rejected option instead of just the top alternative. Change one condition and the cost changes: if the tutoring gig is canceled, napping or studying suddenly costs less, so the choice gets easier. The same logic scales from afternoons to careers: every yes is also a no to your next-best alternative.

answers.output: Caching means keeping a copy of expensive data close at hand — say, a product page's price fetched from the database once and held in memory, so the next 10,000 visitors skip the query. Cache invalidation is deciding when that copy is stale and must be dropped or refreshed. The problem: the cache is a copy, and copies drift from the source. The price changes, but visitors keep seeing the old one. Two common strategies: a TTL — expire the copy after, say, 60 seconds — simple, but there's always a window where users see outdated prices; or active purging — when the price updates, the code also deletes the cache key, so the next request refetches. Active purging is fresher but couples the write path to every cache holding that data. The real difficulty: one piece of data lives in many caches — page cache, CDN, search index — and missing one leaves users with inconsistent data.

answers.output: Compound growth means gains earn gains: each period grows by a percentage of the new, larger total, so value multiplies by (1+r)^n. At 10% a year, $1,000 becomes $1,100, then $1,210 — year two's gain is bigger because it's computed on a bigger base. That's why the starting amount matters — the same rate and time yield ten times the dollars from ten times the seed, which is why early saving gets so much emphasis. Change one condition: stretch 50 years to 60 and the multiplier jumps from 117 to about 304. Because n sits in the exponent, small changes in rate or time swing the outcome enormously.

answers.output: A web page often reads data from a database, which is slowish, so the application keeps a fast copy—the cache—and serves later requests from it. The problem appears the moment the real data changes: the price is updated in the database, but the cache still holds the old one, and customers see stale prices. Cache invalidation is the discipline of deciding when a cached copy is no longer trustworthy and must be dropped or refreshed. The simple approach is a TTL: expire every entry after, say, 60 seconds—cheap, but stale for up to a minute. The careful approach is write-through: whenever the database is updated, also update or delete the cache entry—always fresh, but more code and more failure modes. Every web application lives somewhere on this scale between freshness, speed, and complexity; that is why cache invalidation is famously called one of the hard problems of computer science.

answers.output: Compound growth means growth on growth: each period's gain is added to the base, so the next gain is bigger. At 10% a year, 1,000 becomes 1,100, then 1,210, then 1,331—the yearly increase itself grows from 100 to 121 to 133. The formula is A = P(1+r)^t, and the exponent is the whole story: the same rate applied longer does not add, it multiplies. A handy rule of thumb: money doubles in about 72/r years, so 8% doubles in roughly 9 years. Why the starting amount matters: growth is multiplication, so everything scales by the principal—twice the starting money means twice the final amount, forever, at the same rate. And because time sits in the exponent, starting earlier usually beats saving more later: 1,000 invested 10 years sooner can outgrow 1,500 invested later.

answers.output:
Population variance measures how spread out a whole set of numbers is around its average.

The average alone can hide spread: two classes both average 70, one with everyone between 68 and 72, the other with scores from 30 to 100. Variance is the number that tells them apart.

Compute it in three steps: find the average; take each value's distance from it; square each distance and average the squares. Squaring does two jobs — it stops positive and negative distances from cancelling (scores 5 above and 5 below would otherwise sum to zero and look like 'no spread'), and it makes large deviations dominate: a score 20 away counts four times as much as one 10 away.

The result is in squared units, which is awkward, so people often take the square root (the standard deviation) to return to the original units.

One limitation: variance measures spread around the mean only — one loose cluster and two tight clusters can share the same variance without the same shape.

Opportunity cost is the value of the best option you give up when choosing one option — not all the options you skipped, just the top one among them.

You have a free afternoon: nap, hike, or finish a project. You choose the hike. If finishing the project mattered most to you, that's your opportunity cost; the nap adds nothing, because you could never have done both anyway.

This is why a free afternoon isn't really free: no money changes hands, but you still pay by not doing the next-best thing.

Change one condition: if the project deadline disappears, its value drops, and the nap may become the real opportunity cost — the cost shifts with what you would actually do instead. So when something looks free, ask what you're giving up to get it.

A cache keeps a copy of data close by so you don't re-fetch it every time. A product page is read 10,000 times an hour but changes twice a day — read it from the database once, keep the copy in memory, serve future reads fast.

Invalidation is deciding when that copy is stale and must be dropped. If the price changes in the database but the cache still holds the old one, users see a wrong price.

Main strategies: a fixed time-to-live — simple, but the data can be wrong until expiry; invalidate-on-write — updating the price deletes the cached entry so the next read refetches — accurate, but you must catch every code path that writes the price.

It's called a hard problem because 'when is my copy wrong?' is fundamentally a timing question between two stores that briefly disagree. Every option trades freshness against speed; pick based on how stale users can tolerate.

Compound growth means the gain is computed on the accumulated total, not just the original amount — so gains start earning gains.

At 10% a year: 100 becomes 110, then 121, then 133. Each year's increase grows because the base it multiplies keeps growing. After n years: starting × 1.1^n. Simple growth instead adds a flat 10 each year and reaches 200 in ten years; compounding reaches 100 × 1.1^10 ≈ 259, and the gap widens every year.

The starting amount matters because the same factor multiplies it: 1,000 at 10% becomes about 2,594 in ten years, while 100 becomes only 259. Same rate, same waiting — ten times the outcome, because the exponent acts on whatever you begin with.

Two conditions: losses compound too (−50% needs +100% to recover), and time is what makes the exponent bite — most of the total comes from the final years, which is why starting early outweighs starting big.

If you choose the gym, the cost isn't 'napping AND moving'; you could only have done one of the others anyway, so the cost is whichever of those you'd realistically have done — say, the nap. answers.output: Two classes can have the same average height, say 170 cm, yet feel completely different: in one, everyone is between 168 and 172; in the other, heights range from 150 to 190. Variance is the number that captures this difference in spread. Recipe: subtract the mean from every value, square each deviation, then average those squares. Squaring is the key move — plain deviations always sum to zero, positives canceling negatives — so we square to make everything positive and punish large misses extra hard. One caveat: a single extreme outlier dominates the sum of squares, so variance is very sensitive to rare extremes.

answers.output: A cache keeps a copy of slow-to-fetch data close by so pages load fast — but a copy can go stale. Cache invalidation means finding and discarding copies when the real data changes. Say your app caches product prices so pages render in milliseconds. The store cuts a price from ¥99 to ¥79, but the cache still says 99, so shoppers see — or pay — the old number. Three common remedies: update the cache along with the database (write-through); delete the cached entry and let the next request re-fetch fresh data (invalidate-on-write); or give every copy an expiry time, say 60 seconds, after which it self-destructs (TTL). The trade-off never changes: freshness versus speed. Expiry too long leaves stale prices for minutes; too short hammers the database and the cache stops earning its keep. It is considered hard because changes can come from anywhere — admin edits, other services, batch jobs — and every cached copy must hear about each one.

answers.output: Compound growth means gains themselves start earning gains. Simple interest pays only on the original amount; compound interest pays on the running total, so growth feeds growth. At 10% a year, ¥10,000 becomes ¥11,000, then ¥12,100 — the yearly gain itself grows. The formula is A = P(1+r)^t: starting amount P, rate r, years t; time sits in the exponent, so money multiplies by (1+r) every year without slowing. Why the starting amount matters: the rate fixes everyone's multiplier, not everyone's outcome. Over 30 years at 10%, both ¥10,000 and ¥1,000 grow about 17.4×, but the absolute gap widens from ¥9,000 to roughly ¥157,000 — differences compound too. Two practical notes: small rate changes also act exponentially, so a few percentage points over decades matter enormously; and the curve looks flat early, with most of the total arriving near the end, which is why people underestimate compounding.

answers.output: Cache invalidation is the problem of keeping a fast copy from disagreeing with the slow source of truth. A web app caches the product price in memory: reads take 1 ms instead of a 50 ms database hit. When the price changes in the database, the cached copy is stale—users still see the old price. Invalidation is deciding when and how to drop or refresh that copy. Three common strategies: TTL (expire after 60 seconds—simple, but data can be stale for up to 60 s); delete-on-write (update the database, then remove the cache key so the next read repopulates it fresh); write-through (update cache and database together on every write). The hard part is scale: with many cache nodes and many writers, figuring out which copies are now wrong gets genuinely difficult—that is why people joke it is one of the two hard problems in computer science. Change one condition: if prices must never be wrong for even a second, TTL alone cannot deliver; you need write-time invalidation.

answers.output: Two classes both average 60: one has every student at 60, the other mixes 20s and 100s. The average hides that difference; variance measures it. Recipe: subtract the mean from each value (its deviation), square each deviation, then average the squares. For {20, 60, 100}: mean 60, deviations −40, 0, 40, squares 1600, 0, 1600, so variance = 3200/3 ≈ 1067. Squaring does two jobs: without it, deviations cancel out (+40 and −40 would sum to zero, wrongly suggesting no spread), and it makes large misses dominate the number. The unit becomes points², so reports usually take the square root — the standard deviation, here ≈ 33 points, comparable to the original scores. 'Population' variance divides by N, used when you have all the data. Change one value from 100 to 140 and variance jumps sharply — extremes are amplified, which is exactly the point when outliers are what you care about.

answers.output: An opportunity cost is the value of the single best thing you give up. Your free-afternoon options: study for Monday's exam, freelance for $80, nap, hike. You can do only one, so napping costs whichever alternative you valued most — say the exam grade. Two common mistakes: adding up all the other options (you couldn't have done them all anyway), and counting only money spent (the nap is 'free,' but it still costs the afternoon). The cost shifts when conditions shift: if the exam moves to next month, studying loses value and napping gets cheaper. The idea applies wherever options exclude each other — a free concert, a free upgrade of your time, 'just this once.' The real question is never only what you pay, but what you passed on.

answers.output: A cache keeps a copy of expensive data close by so you don't recompute or refetch it every time. Invalidation is deciding when that copy is no longer trustworthy and must be dropped or refreshed. Example: a product page is cached for an hour; the merchant changes the price to $90, but users keep seeing $100 until the copy expires — the cache is stale. Two common policies: give each entry a TTL and let it expire on its own (simple, but there is always a window of wrong answers), or actively delete the entry whenever the data is written (fresher, but every writer must remember to do it). It's called a famously hard problem because a stale copy looks perfectly normal — nothing marks it wrong — so one forgotten invalidation path serves bad data indefinitely. For any cache, ask: when the data changes, who throws the copy away, and how fast must it happen?

answers.output: Compound growth means gains earn gains: each period's growth applies to the accumulated total, not just the original amount. $1,000 at 10% a year becomes $1,100, then $1,210, then $1,331 — after n years, $1,000 × 1.1ⁿ. That multiplication by 1.1ⁿ is exactly why the starting amount matters: the rate multiplies whatever base you begin with. Start with $2,000 and every future value doubles; start ten years earlier and ten extra multiplications turn $1,000 into about $2,594 before you contribute anything new. Initial size and timing act through the two levers of the same product — base and exponent. Change the rate to 0% and compounding vanishes entirely; raise it and gaps between starting points grow proportionally wider. The same feedback structure appears in followers, bacteria, and debt.

answers.output: You have one free afternoon and can pick only one: nap, study, or take a paid shift worth $50. Whatever you choose, its opportunity cost is the value of the single best option you gave up — not all the others added together. If you nap, the cost is $50, since the shift beats studying for you today. If you take the shift, the cost is the rest you wanted most. This is why 'free' time isn't free: an afternoon spent is one of your finite afternoons spent. Two clarifications: cost is measured by the runner-up only, and it's subjective — a burned-out person's cost of working is high. If the paid gig disappears, napping suddenly costs almost nothing. Every 'choose this' silently means 'give up the second-best'.

answers.output: A cache keeps a copy of expensive data — say a product page built from the database — so repeat requests are fast. Invalidation is the problem of keeping that copy consistent with the source: the store lowers the price, but the cache still serves the old page, and customers see a stale price. Standard moves: expire by time (TTL) — accept staleness for at most, say, 60 seconds; invalidate on write — when the price changes, delete the cached entry so the next request rebuilds it. Each trades something: TTL is simple but can show wrong prices for a while; write-invalidation is fresher but couples the cache to every write path. It's famously hard because you must know exactly which stored copies, across many servers, a single underlying change makes wrong.

Time acts similarly: at 10%, money doubles roughly every 7 years (rule of 72: 72 ÷ rate ≈ doubling time). Change the condition: raise r from 10% to 15% and the ten-year factor jumps from 2.59 to 4.05 — small rate differences matter enormously over long horizons.

answers.output: Variance measures how spread out numbers are around their average. Two classes can both average 70, yet one sits between 65 and 75 while the other ranges from 20 to 100 — variance captures that difference. To compute it: take each value's distance from the mean, square each distance, then average the squares — variance = mean of (x − μ)². With values 4 and 6: mean 5, deviations −1 and +1, variance = (1+1)/2 = 1. Why square? Deviations above and below the mean cancel to zero if you just add them, so squaring makes every distance count. Squaring also punishes big outliers harder: one value 10 away contributes 100, while ten values each 1 away contribute 10 total — an emphasis on large deviations, a design choice rather than the only option. Since squaring changes units (points become points²), taking the square root gives the standard deviation, back in original units.

answers.output: Opportunity cost is the value of the best option you gave up — not all options, just the top one you would have picked instead. With a free afternoon you could study for an exam, earn $60 at a shift, or nap. If you choose the shift, your opportunity cost is the exam prep, since that's your next-best use of the time — not "studying plus napping plus everything else." This reframes "free" activities: a free movie still costs whatever else those two hours could have done. No money leaves your pocket, but time is spent either way. Two refinements: compare against the single best alternative only — adding up every forgone option double-counts; and ignore sunk costs — if you already bought a non-refundable ticket, that money is gone regardless, so the real choice is "attend vs. next-best thing," not "get my money's worth." The habit to build: before committing, ask, "compared with what?"

answers.output: A cache stores a copy of data close by so your app doesn't rebuild it on every request. Cache invalidation is deciding when that copy is stale and must be deleted or refreshed. Example: a web store caches each product page — built once, then served from memory to every visitor. When the merchant changes the price, the cached page still shows the old one. Invalidation means deleting that cached page the instant the price updates, so the next request rebuilds it from the database. The hard part is timing: invalidate too rarely and users see wrong prices; too often and the cache stops saving work. Two common policies: expire after 60 seconds (time-based), or delete the key whenever the underlying data changes (event-based). Coverage is the tricky part — one price change also affects the product list, search results, and recommendations; miss one affected key and a stale page survives. That's why invalidation is famously called a hard problem.

answers.output: Compound growth means growth applies to the accumulated total, not just the original amount, so gains themselves start earning gains. At 10% a year, 100 becomes 110 in year 1, but year 2 adds 11 — interest charged on 110, not 100. The formula is 100 × 1.10ⁿ: the exponent turns steady percentages into acceleration. 1.10¹⁰ ≈ 2.59, so ten years gives 259, not 200; at 20%, 1.20¹⁰ ≈ 6.19. Why the starting amount matters: with the same rate and time, results scale proportionally. Growing at 10% for ten years, 1,000 becomes 2,590 and 10,000 becomes 25,900 — identical percentage growth, very different absolute gains, because compound growth multiplies whatever base you give it; a bigger base is simply more principal for the exponent to act on. The same logic explains why early contributions win: money deposited sooner compounds through more years, so 1,000 saved now outranks 1,000 saved a decade later.

answers.output: An average tells you the center; variance tells you how spread out the values are around that center. Two classes can both average 70 — one with everyone at 70, another with 40s and 90s — and the average alone hides this. Variance: take each value's distance from the mean, square it, then average the squares. Squaring matters: raw distances cancel out (+20 and −20 sum to zero), while squares make every deviation count and punish big ones extra. Example: values 60, 70, 80, mean 70; deviations −10, 0, +10; squares 100, 0, 100; variance = 200/3 ≈ 67. Units are squared, so √variance (the standard deviation) returns to original units. Condition change: add 10 to every value — deviations stay the same, so variance stays the same: it measures spread, not location. Push the 80 out to 100 and variance jumps sharply, because squares emphasize outliers.

answers.output: Opportunity cost is the value of the best option you give up. Say your free afternoon has three uses: nap, gym, or a movie with a friend. If you pick the gym, the cost isn't all the others — only the single best one you didn't take, say the nap. This shows cost doesn't require money; time is the scarce resource. The judgment rule: choose an option only if its value beats the best forgone alternative. Condition change: if the friend is leaving town tomorrow, the movie's value jumps, so the gym's opportunity cost rises and may no longer be worth it. Common mistake: counting every rejected option as cost — you could only have taken one anyway. Transfer: deciding whether to binge a show, don't ask what else you could possibly do; ask what the single best thing you are giving up is — usually the sleep or exercise you actually needed.

answers.output: A cache keeps a copy of data close by so you don't recompute or re-fetch it every time. A product page read 10,000 times an hour but changed twice a day makes a database fetch on every visit pure waste — so you cache it. Cache invalidation is deciding when that copy is no longer trustworthy and must be dropped or refreshed. The core danger: cache and source disagree, and users see stale data — a customer updates their address, but the page still shows the old one. Common strategies: set a time-to-live and accept up to, say, 60 seconds of staleness; or invalidate on write — when the data changes, delete the cache entry so the next read re-fetches fresh data; often both are combined. The hard part is coverage: miss one code path that writes the data, and its stale copy can live on indefinitely — which is why cache invalidation is famously called one of the hard problems in computer science.

answers.output: Compound growth means each period's gain is computed on the accumulated total, not just the original. Put $100 at 10% per year: year 1 adds $10; year 2's 10% applies to $110, adding $11. After 10 years you have 100 × 1.1¹⁰ ≈ $259. Because the base keeps growing, the gains themselves grow — that is compounding. The starting amount matters because multiplication preserves ratios: the same rate and time turn $1,000 into $2,590. And the absolute gap widens — after 10 years the difference is $2,331, not the initial $900, since the larger balance earns larger gains every period. Condition change: time amplifies everything — at 20 years, $100 becomes $673. A quick check: at r% per period, money doubles in roughly 72/r periods. But losses compound too: a −50% year needs +100% to recover.

answers.output: 似然回答的是：'假如某个假设为真，看到手头这批数据的可能性有多大？'它是条件概率 P(数据|假设)，方向是假设→数据。例子：口袋里两枚硬币，甲是公平币（正面概率0.5），乙两面都是正面。连抛三次全是正面。P(三正|甲)=0.5³=0.125，P(三正|乙)=1——这两个数就是似然。固定同一批数据、变换假设，似然用来比较哪个假设让数据显得不奇怪。它不是'假设为真的概率'，那是后验 P(假设|数据)，方向反过来，两者由贝叶斯公式相连：后验 ∝ 似然×先验。若事先抽到两枚的机会各半，则 P(乙|三正)=(1×0.5)/(1×0.5+0.125×0.5)≈0.89。数据偏向乙，但结论掺着先验：先验越偏向甲，同样的数据把后验拉向乙就越慢。似然大只说明数据支持它，不等于它已经为真。

answers.output: A cache keeps a copy of slow data next to fast code — say, the product price held in memory instead of querying the database on every page view. Reads get fast, but now the price lives in two places and they can disagree: the merchant changes it to $80, the database updates, yet the cache still says $100. answers.output: A cache keeps a copy of data close by so you don't pay to fetch or recompute it on every request. Invalidation is the rule for throwing that copy away when the real data changes. Example: a product's price changes in the database, but the page was cached and still shows $20 — until that copy is invalidated, every visitor sees a wrong price. answers.output: The average gives the center of the data; variance measures how far values spread around that center. For a whole population: σ² = (1/N) Σ (xᵢ − μ)². Take each value, subtract the mean μ (its deviation), square it, then average the squares. Example: {4, 5, 6} has mean 5, deviations −1, 0, 1, variance (1+0+1)/3 ≈ 0.67. {0, 5, 10} has the same mean but variance (25+0+25)/3 ≈ 16.7 — same center, far more spread. Squaring serves two jobs: it stops +1 and −1 from cancelling to zero, and it punishes large deviations harder. The price: units get squared (kg²), so we usually take the square root — the standard deviation — to return to kg. Why squares rather than absolute values? Both remove signs; squaring is the conventional choice, smooth and mathematically convenient, not a logical necessity. It also makes variance sensitive to outliers: replace 6 with 100 and it explodes.

answers.output: A cache keeps a nearby copy of slow-to-fetch data — say the rendered profile page — so repeat visits are fast. The catch: the user edits their bio, but the cache still holds the old page, and visitors see stale data. Cache invalidation is removing or refreshing such stale copies so the cache matches the source of truth. Two common strategies. TTL: every entry expires after, say, 60 seconds — simple, but data can be stale for up to a minute, and the database absorbs the refresh load. Active invalidation: when the user saves a new bio, the app explicitly deletes the cached profile — fresh immediately, but you must catch every write path, including admin edits and batch jobs; miss one and users see stale data indefinitely. That is why it's called one of the hard problems of computing: the copy must track a source it doesn't control.

answers.output: Population variance measures how spread out a set of numbers is around their mean. Recipe: find the mean μ, subtract it from every value to get deviations, square each deviation, then average the squares. Formula: σ² = (1/N) Σ(xᵢ − μ)². Example: scores 4, 6, 8 have mean 6; deviations are −2, 0, 2; squares are 4, 0, 4; variance = (4+0+4)/3 ≈ 2.67. Why square? Raw deviations always sum to zero (they cancel out), and squaring makes every deviation count while punishing large departures more heavily. The units are squared, so taking the square root gives the standard deviation, which is back in the original units.

answers.output: An average tells you the center of a set of numbers, but not how spread out they are. Two classes can both average 70: one where everyone scores 68–72, another with scores from 40 to 99. Variance measures that spread. Recipe: (1) take each value and subtract the average — this is its deviation from center; (2) square each deviation (multiplying it by itself); (3) average those squared deviations. We square for two reasons: negative deviations would otherwise cancel positive ones and sum to zero, and large deviations get extra weight, which is usually what we want. answers.output: A cache is a fast local copy of data that's expensive to fetch (e.g., your app stores a user's profile in memory or Redis instead of hitting the database every time). Cache invalidation is the problem of keeping that copy correct: when the underlying data changes, the cached copy becomes stale and must be deleted or refreshed. The three common strategies: (1) TTL — expire entries after, say, 60 seconds; simple, but data can be stale in between. (2) Invalidate on write — whenever you update the database, delete the matching cache key so the next read reloads fresh data. (3) Write-through — update cache and database together. It's famously hard because in a distributed system there are many cache copies and 'when exactly should each be dropped?' has no perfect answer — hence the saying that cache invalidation is one of the two hard problems in computer science.

answers.output: A cache stores copies of expensive-to-compute data (like a database query) so the next request is fast. Cache invalidation is the problem of making sure those copies don't go stale when the underlying data changes. Example: your app caches a user's profile page for 10 minutes. If the user changes their bio, visitors may see the old bio until the cache expires. Basic strategies: (1) TTL — expire entries after a fixed time; simple, but data can be stale until then. The hard part: one piece of data may feed many cached pages, and distributed caches make timing tricky — hence the saying 'there are only two hard things in computer science: cache invalidation and naming things.' Rule of thumb for beginners: start with short TTLs, and invalidate explicitly on writes where staleness matters.

answers.output: An average tells you the center of a set of numbers; variance tells you how spread out they are around that center. To compute it: find the mean, subtract it from every value to get each deviation, square each deviation (so negatives don't cancel positives), then average those squares. Example: {4, 4, 4, 4} and {1, 7, 1, 7} both have mean 4. The first set has variance 0—every value equals the mean. The second: deviations are -3, 3, -3, 3; squares are 9, 9, 9, 9; variance = 36/4 = 9. Bigger variance means values typically wander further from the average. Note the units are squared (if data is in kg, variance is kg²); taking the square root gives the standard deviation, which is back in original units.

answers.output: Opportunity cost is the value of the best alternative you give up when you choose one option. You have a free afternoon: you could study for an exam, go to the gym, nap, or meet a friend. If you choose studying, the opportunity cost is not 'all the other three options'—it's specifically the one you would most likely have done instead, say going to the gym. You spent no money, but you still paid a cost: the afternoon itself. Reasoning this way improves decisions—don't just ask 'is this option good?', ask 'is it better than my next-best use of this time?' That's why 'free' things aren't truly free: your time always has alternative uses.

answers.output: A cache is a fast temporary copy of data kept close to your application—say, the result of an expensive database query, or a rendered page—so repeat requests skip the slow work. The problem: the underlying data changes. If a user updates their profile but the cached page still shows the old one, they see stale data. Cache invalidation is the process of removing or refreshing cached entries when the source data changes, so the next request rebuilds it fresh. Common strategies: TTL (each entry expires after N seconds, simple but serves stale data until then); write-through (update cache and database together); and delete-on-write (when data changes, evict the cache key so it's recomputed). It's famously called one of the hardest problems in computer science because knowing exactly which entries to invalidate, and when, gets tricky as data dependencies grow.
